utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the cord exploded -- before it explodes, the detonation wave is extremely fast and has already started with the detonator -- the explosion of the detonator before the explosion of the whole charge, the detonator may probably make some stones or bits of rock crumble, which after that -- should I repeat? This is my impression, that's my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You've indicated that the water pillar we see in TV Mostar is not the same water pillar that we see in TV ORF, and I just want to momentarily go back to TV ORF so you can see that water pillar again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you see it right there at 1.4?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you'll agree with me and you testified yesterday that what we see on the screen now resembles what you later tried to replicate in your experiment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, on the frame one can see there is the water wall which is fairly long, but one can also see at the level of surface of the water small splashes on the left of the water wall. Would this correspond to the splashing on the other video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think it's the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, you have now indicated at least 15 times the issue of whether these two events are the same or different. Yesterday I already recited for you at least over ten times in which you indicated that they were the same event, and then yesterday towards the end of the day you indicated that they were a different event. About ten minutes ago you finally agreed that they were a different event, yet you have just testified again that they are the same event. I will ask you one final time, are these water pillars, these events preceding what you believe to be the collapse, the same event or a different event?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can make one observation. In fairness to the witness he did say repeatedly, of course my learned friend is quite correct the way she puts her last question, but, for example, at page 38, line 22, and the witness said very clearly: "To give you my opinion on this video I would have to watch it on my computer, quietly, in slow motion." The witness has said that kind of statement on a number of occasions. Now it's completely proper for my learned friend to test the witness's expertise and the conclusions upon which he bases his report, but to seek to turn the crucible of the courtroom into a laboratory whilst he's surrounded by judiciary, members of the parties, and to look at matters that -- frame by frame when the technology is not available and then to seek to criticize him for some conclusions, when he said very properly this is not a laboratory, very properly that he needs time to look at it on a frame-by-frame basis is perhaps a little bit unfair. Of course the witness can give his instinctive reactions in the same way that we all have our own views from looking at the evidence without any degree of scientific or technical analysis, but it's my submission that may not be of an awful lot of assistance to Your Honours. Your Honour, that's the observation I do make.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, maybe there is a linguistic problem. You express yourself in French which has, of course, qualifications and is very precise. When you say the same splash, the same event, in your mind is the fact that there are two splashes in two different videos correspond to the same event or do you say that the two splashes we've seen are two different events? Could you be specific on that, because sometimes English does not cross exactly the nuance of the French language. So when you speak of these splashes, same splashes, are you talking about the same event or are you saying there are two splashes and they are two different events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will start by the beginning if I may. I say that it is one event, one splash, in the two cases when we wrote our report. I've been shown here something which features clearly -- by the way, something -- I've seen here something I haven't been able to analyse. To say that two splashes are the same I have to analyse them because the same splash seen by two different cameras, I have to -- they are seen from a different angle but it is one splash or one pillar. Is it the same although it is seen from a different angle because there are two different cameras which have recorded this? That is one point. Therefore, I couldn't do that. But as you will have noticed, I have been requested to give a yes or no opinion. I have, therefore, the impression now that those are two splashes: One after which the bridge does not collapse and the other one after which the bridge collapses. But for all this, as I have told you, one has to be able to see peacefully frame by frame --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So to conclude, if one watches the three videos, there are two splashes which correspond or water pillars which correspond to the first event when the bridge does not collapse, therefore it's an attempt which failed; and the second water wall or pillar corresponds to the falling of the bridge and that is an attempt which is successful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is what I think now but without performing an analysis. With all we have here that is what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be of some assistance and since the Prosecution was so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I don't think it's necessary. I think I have perfectly summarized the situation and your witness agrees with my summary. So if you want to add something there will be more confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree precisely because it was summarized. I don't want to appear as if I want to spoil it, quite the contrary is the case, I'm quite happy with the way you summarized it. But in this regard I would like to say something because I will not be raising this in re-direct. At page 8 to 10 of the document that was disclosed to us today, there is a chapter that for the most part confirms your argument, your summary. But we cannot now go into that. I just wanted to draw your attention to this. I don't know if anyone wants to tender this document into evidence or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So it's the first splash. Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, you've been a professional for a long period of time and so you're familiar with the concept of peer review; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a specific procedure in order to check our colleagues, that's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And yesterday you testified that you welcomed your colleagues to review your work here; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If anybody can help find the truth, of course I shall bow to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, I'm going to direct your attention again to Exhibit 3D 03154, it's in your binder and it's the Hartmann report that we spoke of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You remember Judge Prandler actually asked you some questions about this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You don't remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, nonetheless, do you remember on page 44, line 14, commenting that Professor Hartmann's opinion did not run counter to yours and, in fact, that they went together. Do you remember testifying to that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I explained that regarding the destruction of the bridge with an explosive charge we share the same opinion, Professor Hartmann and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Professor --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, with regard to the destruction of the bridge with projectiles, Professor Hartmann does not know projectile-related specialty, it's not his specialty, he doesn't know that technology.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But nonetheless, you asked Professor Hartmann to make comments on your report, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Who invited him to make the comments?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ask Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. We're going to go to paragraph 3 and we're going to go through this piecemeal. We'll start with the first sentence under paragraph 3. Dr. Hartmann wrote: "According to the material available to me, the actual reasons for the collapse of the bridge are extremely uncertain." Notwithstanding your view of Dr. Hartmann's credential, is it fair to say that he disagrees with your conclusion that the bridge came down because of an explosion via an underwater detonation cord?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Further down, Professor Hartmann said that everything we wrote down was possible and real.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. That's not my question. My question is: According to that sentence, would you agree with me that Professor Hartmann disagrees with your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall repeat. He believes or he sees the destruction of the bridge only from the point of view of explosives. He's not able to assess whether the bridge was destroyed by projectiles. Because he does not know that fact, he's bound to conclude the way he does. I would have done the same. But since I know that the bridge did not collapse because of a projectile, I conclude that there's no other possibility than the explosive.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- all the manifestations of the destructions are shown as by explosive.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, the next sentence is: "However, it is obvious to me that the tank shelling caused enormous destructions to the Old Bridge in Mostar ..." Here Professor Hartmann is speaking about the shelling that happened previously and we saw all of the coverage that happened or much of the coverage that happened on November 8th. Did you consider the previous shelling in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let's be careful. I don't know what elements or what material Professor Hartmann has. I feel that we did not have the same material, but at any rate in the material that we had we looked at all the effects. And as I said, I agree that the bridge had been damaged, but I also draw your attention to the fact that the destruction was mainly on what was built on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, are you testifying that, in fact, you did consider all the previous shelling in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everything we could see in the videos.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you point to me where in your opinion you talk about the previous shelling on November 8th, in your analysis of the videotapes of November 8th?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the text in its French translation. It should be exactly the same as in the English translation. So let me read the French text. "I can see the destruction of the -- because of the HVO tank which can be seen" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking for the page, please. Can we have the page in the translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] English text --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly asked to read slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The fire of the military tank of the Croatian tank [indiscernible] is being held responsible for the destruction of the Old Bridge in the city of Mostar," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, I'll just ask you one question that might make this a little bit more simple. You did not look at extensive videotape from the November 8th shelling, did you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can you show me what you think I didn't see and then I'll tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, it's impossible for me to show you what I think you didn't see. The question is: Did you review extensive videotape from November 8th in order to write your report? The answer is yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we watched a lot of things and out of all this material everything that related to our report is appended in the attachments. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And you'll agree with me that the only thing appended to your report is the TV ORF video, the TV Mostar video, and your experiment video; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at the -- back to Dr. Hartmann's report. If you look at the fourth paragraph, it's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do apologise. This is now the second time my learned friend has characterized the document from Dr. Hartmann as a report. I think that overstates the case. The doctor says in paragraph 2 that he makes only comments, and I quote: "... an official appointment as assessor took not place," that's obviously a mistake in the syntax, "at no point in time. As a consequence, the following annotations remain informal." It is a letter that no doubt my learned friend has disclosed in a spirit of fairness. There's no details from the face of this letter regarding the amount of time Dr. Hartmann spent on this project, and so it does go to the earlier comment regarding peer review. In my submission, it can't properly be put as a report that in any way, shape, or form can be said to gain say in any material in particular the evidence of the witness under oath before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is not my report, this is a report that the Defence admitted yesterday or spoke about yesterday, this is not something that we came up with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think that is not the issue, but I think that counsel is quite right, this is a letter, and the word "report" is putting it too high.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Then I will say letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, I think you should do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may since we have interrupted the testimony. A moment ago when the expert read a couple of sentences from the expert report it was not entered into the transcript because he was reading too fast. Perhaps just a reference, that's at page 3, both in the B/C/S and the French version, that's the second paragraph, I think he read two or three sentences. So just so that we have a reference. So it's page 3 in the French and the English version. And now that I've taken the floor, I didn't want to waste time about what my colleague has just indicated, but I do think that we have to distinguish -- make a distinction here. This is a letter that was sent to me by Dr. Hartmann at my request, nothing else and nothing more than that. This person was not retained as an expert, we do not intend to call him as an expert. We merely wanted to get his opinion. So it is just a letter. You heard that there was a question about any challenges to their expert opinion once the analysis was published I wanted to -- I initiated this in order to see whether there was any criticism of the report. So this is the purpose behind this letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Looking to paragraph 4, the sentence starts with: "Nevertheless, having studied the explanations in the engineering opinion of the aforementioned Zagreb experts, in accordance with the more or less corresponding video sequences, I can establish that the conclusions drawn there with respect to 'water jet caused by detonation of detonation cord' are plausible." Do you see that part of the letter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, but the word is plausible.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, focus on the part of the sentence it's right in the middle, it says: "I can establish ..." Do you see that part?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the sentence that comes after or the words that come after it, you would agree with me this is what Professor Hartmann -- his opinion or his conclusion is would start right there, do you agree with that, would be the rest of that sentence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: He then writes: " ... that the conclusions drawn there," and here he writes "with respect," and he puts in quotes "'water jet caused by detonation of detonation cord' are plausible." Would you agree that the only thing that Dr. Hartmann concurs with is that it is possible that when you put a detonation cord under water it will create a water jet?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think there's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer was not recorded in the transcript, and I clearly heard "yes."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreters didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you confirm that you said yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, two things, there is your expert report and then his letter, your German colleague's letter in which he expresses his opinion. The Prosecutor is very fast, but I would like to go back precisely to what you said which seems to me relevant. This is what you say. "The destruction of the bridge by an HVO tank that was located south of the bridge and west of the Neretva River at about 1.4 kilometre of distance from there, any video or documentation it is obvious that in the morning of the 8th of November from 9.57 hours to 15.52 hours was hit by many projectiles. Therefore, it is very probable that it was hit by the projectile of the said tank. This conclusion can be drawn on the basis of the recorded visual effect of the explosion." So initially you do not rule out that the bridge may have been destroyed by those projectiles based on the videos, but you add this: "However, the footage of the ORF2 footage just before the collapse of the bridge can suggest another cause for the destruction of the old bridge around 10.00 on the 9th of November. This footage showed a linear water gush," et cetera. Therefore, in your opinion initially you mentioned a possible destruction by shelling, but watching the ORF2 video you concluded that it was caused by an explosive charge, by a splash of light, by smoke, and by a water pillar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As confirmed by the TV Mostar video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your colleague must have seen all of your report, and he seems to conclude in his letter that he is just about certain that the water pillar is connected to the detonating cord that caused the water to rise. So he's about a hundred per cent certain. However, as to the certain causes he does not take any stand because his last sentence seemed to say that all causes remain open. We have the English word "open" at the end of the letter. Therefore, everything remains open. Is this how the letter by your colleague can be analysed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the way I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may proceed, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to direct your attention to another page of this same exhibit, the page number is 3D 35-1174, it's the same exhibit but it's the cover letter that went with this --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I believe you have it right in front of you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a cover letter, it's more statements by Professor Hartmann in regard to your report and I'm going to read the first sentence. "In the attachments you will find my statement in which I have taken over most of your adjustments. Further alterations, however, would not suit me. I kindly request you not insist on additional changes." This cover letter was directed to counsel for Mr. Praljak. Since this was based on your own report, were you consulted about the additional changes requested of Hartmann by counsel?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You don't know if you were consulted about those changes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the changes are about.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to go to the next sentence. There he writes: "Due to my limited time and my burden in many current research projects, I would also very much appreciate if you could avoid any future involvement of my person in the case of the prosecution of General Praljak" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may object, Your Honour. If I understand correctly, the witness clearly said, "I don't know at all," so the witness was not involved in my communication with Professor Hartmann. He clearly answered, so he is now asked once again. He cannot be asked when he provided the answer, "I don't know," and if anybody would have to testify on that it would be me. I sent the letter to Professor Hartmann, I got one response, I put additional letter, I got an additional response. So it's not for witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not going to spend the entire winter on this. Now, there was a communication, an exchange, between Professor Hartmann and Mr. Kovacic. Apparently you were not aware of that, but as much as you can remember, at any point in time did Mr. Kovacic call you to tell you that you had to change your report on this or that part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you are saying this under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you raised your hand to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It might be good to break. Judge Trechsel thinks that we can still hold on for another ten minutes. Okay. We'll work until 5.30. Usually it's one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I'd like to draw your attention to page 6 of your report in English. Take your time. Your report. Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've got it, but I think the numbering is not the same. I mean, I have a copy from my computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can somebody help me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just in front of you, you can see the picture on your screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have six frames, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These frames come from TV Mostar, from that video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see water activity, splashes, but I fail to see a water wall because it's -- the focus is too narrow. Is there any reason why you thought that here as well there was a water wall, a long water wall, as can be seen in the ORF video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. We discussed this very issue, and our conclusion was that it cannot be seen here, not because it does not exist but because the vantage point is much to the left. You can't see all of the water wall, you see only part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at the bottom right frame.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's just at already the end because you have 1.88 seconds, so nearly 2 seconds have elapsed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you compare these frames with ORF2 frames to see how that is at around the same time, like 1.88?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember we did carry out the comparison for the -- and the results thereof were good for the splash time that our worry is that the bridge did not fall fast enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a second question. Take the next page in your report. There's a small sketch showing your thesis of the detonating cord.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, we saw all this in the video showing the first event. And in your theory, shortly thereafter there was a second event causing apparently the bridge to collapse. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what we were saying earlier on, that there were two water splashes or walls. Well, that's the logical conclusion based on everything we saw here in court, not in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two things. Firstly, is it probable and feasible to place under water two detonating cords? Second question: If you activate one, how probable is it that the second would explode as well because suddenly there is an enormous pressure that is released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely what I was thinking myself, but I'm not a professional in the use of explosives. But I know that very often you have various chain, as it were, of cords to make sure that if one fails there's another chain that you can try to make it work. That's my opinion. If there was a main charge there could be two detonators, two detonating cords. The first was activated and it failed, then the second was activated and it worked. That's possible, but I can't guarantee that it's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you cannot say whether the activation of the first detonating cord may have caused the second cord to be activated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first did not activate the main charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that, but I'm worried about the two explosive detonating cords. And normally, an explosion will have some kind of contagious effect. If you have an explosion and other explosives nearby, more often than not the other explosives will also produce a blast which accounts for some disasters. If you had put two cords, two detonating cords, you would have put them far away from one another, far apart, because one could damage the other, that's for sure. So the other cord was somewhere else, in another position, maybe some metres away, I don't know, maybe some tens of metres away, but not really next to one another. In the same water does it help, is there not any shock wave that would transmit faster than air?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't think so. The fact that one explodes is not going to influence the other provided they are sufficiently far apart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you carried out any experiments on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but I'm aware of the physics of explosives so that's what I say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on the footage we have, is it possible to see that there would be several metres between one and the other hypothetical cords?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is possible, that could be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it cannot -- no trace can be seen of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you have to analyse all that. It would be too risky to say anything, to provide an answer like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Kovacic, did you have any re-direct or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, maybe a couple. I think it might be a good idea to have a break now, which is necessary at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we'll be very brief. We've looked at the transcript, we have some special questions, including references to your own questions. All that will not be necessary, actually. There is one thing that I would like to raise, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Jankovic, you still have the OTP binder in front of you, don't you; if not, I'm sure someone can hand you a set.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it. I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have Ms. Usher's assistance, please. [In English] Okay. Take it. Could you please assist me, usher, document number P 10515.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, there is a letter there, an opinion. First you have the English translation. If you keep on leafing through it you will find the Croatian, a total of two pages. There is something there that wasn't copied properly, and then you have the Croatian text in the upper right corner, the last three digits 558, you can see that that's where it begins, that's page 1. 558 and 559, 560. As far as I remember, some time ago I sent you a copy of this letter as soon as I got it. Please have a look to see if you still remember it. This was sometime in September 2007.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I'm not sure I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Fine. I'm not entirely certain that I forwarded it to you. I thought that I had, but it's a very brief one so we can go through it. I would like to draw your attention to the title itself: "A position on the analysis of the destruction of the Old Bridge in Mostar based on video footage." And then there is a description there, table of contents, and then something that reads basis or foundation or background and you can see Professor Melzer's qualifications and the material that you used and then the situation and the description of the bridge and so on and so forth. Can I draw your attention to something on page 559, that's page 2 in your copy, paragraph 5 towards the bottom of the page. A position taken based on such analysis as is available, the situation, the description of the bridge, you see what he is talking about here. If you look at paragraph 5 Dr. Melzer states: "Having closely studied the analysis," which is referenced as number 1, that is your analysis, pages 1 through 15, "I have not identified any significant technical inaccuracies ." And then: "The flash at the abutment cannot be identified. We can also say that before the fall of the bridge instead of one there were two separate explosions. The reason for that is probably the lower frame frequency (25 frames per second) and the editing methods used in the available video-clips (the video-clips available to me, the so-called fields have also been reconstructed, so that effectively the number of frames per second is 50)." And then on the next page, another two sentences that read: "Nevertheless, the conclusions reached in analysis 1 are certainly technically correct." And then he goes on to state: "Following my own examination of the available video recordings, I can now fully endorse the statements made in analysis 1," and that is your finding. Professor, do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, I'm happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you go back to page 1 and you look at the header, Dr. Rainer Melzer, a civil engineer, office for building and destroying the buildings and facilities; do you perhaps know this person?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear from him and the first time I see this document, the first time I hear about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you have any doubts speaking of this introduction that it is your analysis that he's focusing on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing to doubt about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the next page 3962, we have it in English, Professor Melzer wrote a letter to me in reply to my letter to him. Perhaps I should provide an explanation for the benefit of the Chamber. This opinion is very precise and it fully endorses the analysis that we are now tendering into evidence --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that we're about to get into the same thing that we got into on the Hartmann report. He's now talking about a cover letter that was sent to counsel that this witness has never seen also the witness has never seen this particular report. The second thing is this is an expert report under 94 bis which I would submit he has not complied with the Rules on and cannot now admit it through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Prosecutor, about Mr. Hartmann's letter, you quoted it so you have to allow the Defence to use the letter of Dr. Rainer without quoting 94 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Hartmann letter was produced by counsel to us. He indicated to us for the proceedings that it was not going to be admitted as an expert report. We had some discussions about this. However, this is quite different in that this -- he is calling it a report, it is truly an expert report that he's now trying to admit. So it's not complying with Rule 94 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just respond to this objection, to this objection, it's not new to me -- the letter from the OTP during my preparation, but it wasn't about this, it was about Professor Hartmann's letter that we were looking at a while ago. I would like to respond in purely legal terms. Provisions of Rule 94 bis say that a party, the Defence here, is entitled to move for an expert opinion to be tendered into evidence or not. I haven't done so yet in the case of this opinion because that would probably mean that we would need to call this gentleman to prove him and so on and so forth, which we believe to be entirely unnecessary bearing in mind that we already have an expert report by qualified experts. The idea was precisely about this and I think the witness mentioned this yesterday in part at least, and that is why I picked it up today. This was the idea. There were no reactions from any qualified researchers after the book was published on the Old Bridge which included their own analysis or study. We were concerned by this absence of reactions. As Defence counsel I wanted some form of criticism, I wanted some sort of a reaction, in order to be able to reassure myself that the analysis was technically sound or perhaps that it displayed certain weaknesses, were there certain questions that should be raised, that sort of thing. In this way, we eventually reached two experts in Germany. One was Professor Hartmann, the other was Professor Melzer, two experts that I exchanged letters with. I had received tips from other people who were insiders, but these details are not so important. I asked them several questions. This is the expert report, please criticize, please spot any weaknesses if you can, do you agree, can you endorse this or not. I am not tendering this as an expert report. There is no reason for me to be tendering this as an expert report. What I am, doing simply because the witness referred to this document, I asked a couple of relevant questions, I showed the witness the document, the Professor agreed with the finding in this document. And if we look at the details of the document, it entirely tallies with all the evidence that we've been looking at over the last three days here in the courtroom. This is all directly linked. And I will be moving for this exhibit to be admitted into evidence. I think based on the Chamber's practice so far there shouldn't be any problems with this document becoming an exhibit. Its authenticity is beyond challenge, it definitely has probative value, it's relevant in relation to our case in every way, and by way of a conclusion it was the OTP that tabled this document because they were the ones who placed this in the witness's binder. They brought this on themselves. All I'm doing is reacting to this letter, otherwise you might end up asking yourself why aren't we using this. That is my proposition. I think we are free to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Prosecutor, since there is going to be an IC number with a list of documents which will be -- for which you will request admission, you may request it for this document of Dr. Rainer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just want to ensure that I am clear as to this particular report. The Office of the Prosecutor is not requesting the admission of this report from Dr. Melzer, I understand that counsel is requesting that admission. What I am pointing out is that it is an expert report that was not provided to us under 94 bis, so it has not complied with the Rules and should not be admitted in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if it assists, but the other way of looking at matters, of course, is that -- and I believe my learned friend for General Praljak alluded to it. It may be that the report that's under discussion need not be admitted for the truth of its contents, but of course it can be admitted on another basis. My learned friend in a way, in my respectful submission, opened the door when she sought to put the Hartmann letter to the witness to impugn his findings in part under the rubric of peer review. In that context it may well be the case that the new report can be used to evaluate the credibility of the witness under the same rubric of peer review whilst not being evidence for the truth of its contents. Your Honour, I don't know if that assists as a way forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank my learned friend for lending me his support and handing me another argument in my favour. One thing I would like to point out is that the Defence disclosed to the OTP all of our materials on the 31st of March and over the next following days in a variety of different media, that was after the Rule 65 list was already concluded. We gave them everything we had all at the same time And that was how they got this letter. It was part of my sets of documents. There is no surprise factors involved. Secondly, it is the OTP that who placed this document on the list of documents which they wanted to use during their cross-examination. Thirdly, what my colleague has just underlined, the fact itself that it was the OTP who chose to use the Hartmann document as some sort of an endorsement, and I'm using this on redirect. This is also an endorsement of the expert opinion. It is not in itself an expert opinion or a finding; it is a mere endorsement. It is a document that the Chamber must bear in mind when assessing the expert report before us and all of the evidence provided by this witness. I think this is in the interests of justice. I don't think there should be any procedural intricacies standing in the way, especially not Rule 94 bis. If I wanted 94 bis, I would go for 94 bis, but I definitely have no need at all to take that step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... finished. Very well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, yes, this completes my re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, I would like to take this opportunity to thank you for coming here, to make this enormous effort not just on behalf of General Praljak's Defence but also on behalf of my other colleagues here, my learned friends and the Chamber itself. I thank you very much for coming here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. Your testimony is now finished. I wish to thank you in the name of my colleagues who have come to The Hague to bring your contribution in order to find the truth, and you have my best wishes for your future activities and I shall request from Mrs. Usher to accompany you out of this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we adjourn, since we won't have other witnesses this week, Mr. Prlic's witness will come next week as foreseen. I will tell you that the Appeals Chamber, if you don't know, has rendered its decision on the motion concerning determining the time allotted and the Appeals Chamber confirmed the decision made by our Chamber and rejected the appeals of the several Defence teams. So you will certainly read the judgement maybe this afternoon. Therefore, if there is nothing else on the agenda -- I think Mr. Scott wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, good afternoon. Two things, Your Honour, and I'll take them -- the one item of business, but while I'm on my feet, just on the last point that's been made this afternoon in terms of this last document. I just want to make it very clear the Prosecution position is that this is an entirely improper way to introduce evidence. The fact that it may or may not have been listed as a cross-examination exhibit means absolutely nothing. It may or may not have been proper for cross-examination, but since it was never used, it has no bearing on the question. The Rules provide specific means for the introduction of evidence. One of them, for example, is 92 bis, a witness who -- a party wants to call and the witness has to come for cross-examination or not. But this is a whole new vehicle: Testimony by letter, testimony by vouching letter, and there is no provision in the Rules for that. If Mr. Kovacic wants to file a Rule 92 bis motion to introduce in that manner and the Prosecution can respond and request cross-examination or if he wants to propose it as a 94 bis expert, we will certainly ask for cross-examination, but there is no -- there is no procedure whatsoever for admitting evidence by letter to vouch for the testimony of another witness. That's basically -- that's fundamentally wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order not to lose time, Mr. Praljak's Defence may perhaps, I'm not sure, put this exhibit in its IC list so then you will have the possibility to challenge in writing. So don't pursue on this issue. You will have the opportunity to do so in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I want to make it clear, Your Honour, that I think it was improper to put it to the witness at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be even clearer if it's in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That doesn't address the point, Your Honour, but we will address it in writing, but the information should never have been put before the Chamber, that was improper. That's my point. Number two, I would -- as the Chamber will be aware, there have been a number of applications made for provisional release. I don't know that they've all -- all six accused have now made them, I think not. I think four -- maybe four, perhaps five have filed, but there's one or two that have not yet filed, I think. What the Prosecution would ask the Chamber to do in the interest of efficiency and ask the Chamber to entertain, either inquire of the Defence or ask the Chamber to entertain, a dead-line for the filing of all such motions and then what the Prosecution would like to do is file a single -- a single consolidated response with -- once we have them all, I would ask to make our response within 14 days, the normal time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there are several requests for provisional release which have been filed, not all of them. So I don't know for the moment who are the Defence teams who haven't done so yet, but I invite you, for those who haven't done so yet, to do so so that the Prosecution can file a consolidated reply so that the Chamber may render its decisions. There will be six decisions, all this takes time and I will remind you that we have to finish around the 24th of July. Therefore, all those who are lagging are requested to file as quickly as possible so that Mr. Scott may in the next 14 days file his own motion. I know that, Mr. Scott, even if the Rules give you 14 days -- well, the earlier it will be done the better it will be in order to enable the Chamber to make its six decisions. So I think everything has now been seen and we shall meet again next Monday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
